name: Glen plaid suit

lead: Glen plaid (also called Glen Urquhart or Prince of Wales check) is a woven twill pattern of small and large checks, usually in black or grey with white or in muted colours. A suit made in it is a patterned alternative to a plain navy or grey suit.

For appearance, the pattern gives a suit visual interest and a heritage look, and it has been worn by well-known figures from Edward VIII to Cary Grant. It changes how an outfit reads rather than the body underneath.

paras: It is worn as a full suit, as a sport coat or jacket, or in shirting, and appears in wool and other fabrics. Men choose it to add pattern and texture to tailored clothing.

Clothing carries no health risks beyond fit and comfort. Its look has drawn mixed comment: Ronald Reagan's gray-and-blue glen plaid suit was called 'unpresidential' on a 1982 European trip, and Pee-wee Herman was known for a light-grey one.

angle.text: A glen plaid suit changes how an outfit looks by adding a subtle woven check to tailored clothing. It is a style choice that sits within a man's overall presentation, alongside fit, colour and grooming.

lead: Glen plaid, short for Glen Urquhart plaid, is a woollen twill fabric woven in an irregular check of small and large squares. Two dark and two light stripes alternate with four dark and four light stripes, so the design reads as a crossing check. It is typically black or grey with white, or in muted colours, and the same weave can be used in cotton shirting and other fabrics [1].

The pattern is named for the Glenurquhart Estate in Inverness-shire, Scotland, where the Countess of Seafield reportedly used it in the 1840s to outfit her gamekeepers. As Prince of Wales, King Edward VII made the check famous and Edward VIII later popularised it, which is why it is also called the Prince of Wales check [1].
A glen plaid suit uses the pattern for the whole garment. People wear it to add texture and a classic, tailored look to an outfit, as seen on Cary Grant in North by Northwest (1959) [1].

paras: The weave is a twill in which alternating bands of dark and light threads (two and two, then four and four) cross to form a mix of small and large checks. It is used mainly in wool but also in shirting and other textiles [1].

The name refers to Glenurquhart Estate, where the Countess of Seafield reportedly used the pattern in the 1840s to outfit gamekeepers. The phrase 'Glen plaid' does not appear in print before 1926. Edward VII, as Prince of Wales, brought the check to prominence and Edward VIII popularised it further, despite the Welsh-sounding name [1].

Cary Grant wore a grey suit in subtle glen plaid in North by Northwest (1959). Pee-wee Herman was identified with a light-grey glen plaid suit, and Ronald Reagan was called 'unpresidential' for wearing a gray-and-blue one on a 1982 European trip. Glen plaid tweed sport coats appeared on screen in the 1999 Animal Farm film and in a Doctor Who episode with Matt Smith [1].
